title: AIO: An Abstraction for Performance Analysis Across Diverse Accelerator Architectures
problem: Current performance analysis abstractions for accelerators are mismatched: high-level approaches miss key performance phenomena while low-level approaches focus on details that don't generalize across different accelerator types, making early evaluation of new architectures difficult.
motivation: As specialization becomes critical for post-Dennard scaling performance, continuous proposals of new accelerator architectures require efficient early-stage performance analysis to guide developer and architect efforts productively.
method: The Architecture-Independent Operation (AIO) abstraction represents the parallelizable work in an algorithm—computations that can run simultaneously on multiple data items—in a form that stays the same across different accelerator types (GPU, FPGA, ASIC, etc.). The AccMe tool predicts how fast code will run by estimating clock cycles for three components: computation, memory access, and kernel invocation overhead (the cost of launching the kernel). It accounts for compute-memory overlap (computation happening while data is fetched) and memory bandwidth constraints (the limit on how much data can flow from memory per cycle).
key_novelty: The Architecture-Independent Operation (AIO) identifies the parallelizable algorithm work (computations running simultaneously on multiple data items) that stays the same across different accelerator types (GPU, FPGA, ASIC).
contributions: AIO abstraction enabling unified performance analysis across diverse accelerator types
AccMe performance model achieving 5.6% average prediction error versus 20.6% for Roofline
Demonstrated application to accelerator selection, scheduling optimization (2.8× throughput improvement), and architectural exploration
primary_theme: unified performance modeling for diverse accelerators
